title: Ἀθήνης ἄφοδος
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Nestor ends his long reply by warning Telemachus not to stay away from home for long while the suitors eat up his goods, and sends him on to Menelaus in Lacedaemon, offering a chariot and one of his own sons as escort. As night falls Athena, still in the shape of Mentor, has the tongues burnt and the libations poured and turns to go back to the ship, but Nestor will not hear of a son of Odysseus sleeping on a ship's deck, so she leaves Telemachus in his care and departs in the likeness of a bird of prey. The old man sees that she was a goddess, prays to her and promises her a heifer with gilded horns, then leads the company home, mixes an old wine for a last libation, and puts Telemachus to bed in the portico beside his son Peisistratus before he himself goes to rest beside his wife.

sentences.t:
καὶ σύ, φίλος, μὴ δηθὰ δόμων ἄπο τῆλ’ ἀλάλησο,
κτήματά τε προλιπὼν ἄνδρας τ’ ἐν σοῖσι δόμοισιν
οὕτω ὑπερφιάλους, μή τοι κατὰ πάντα φάγωσιν
κτήματα δασσάμενοι, σὺ δὲ τηϋσίην ὁδὸν ἔλθῃς.
sentences.tr:
kai sy, philos, mē dētha domōn apo tēl’ alalēso,
ktēmata te prolipōn andras t’ en soisi domoisin
houtō hyperphialous, mē toi kata panta phagōsin
ktēmata dassamenoi, sy de tēÿsiēn hodon elthēis.
sentences.l:
You too, friend, do not long, away from home, far off go wandering,
leaving behind both your possessions and men in your house
so overbearing, lest they eat up everything,
having divided your possessions, and you go a fruitless journey.
sentences.i: You too, my friend, do not wander long and far from home, leaving your possessions behind and men so overbearing in your house, for fear that they divide your possessions among them and eat up everything, and your journey turns out fruitless.
sentences.n: The part opens inside Nestor's long reply to Telemachus, begun at 3.254, so there is no opening quotation mark here. καὶ σύ, φίλος opened his lesson from the Orestes story at 3.199 and keeps the same English. μὴ … ἀλάλησο is a prohibition with the perfect imperative middle of ἀλάομαι 'wander'. δόμων ἄπο shows anastrophe, and τῆλ’ is τῆλε 'far'. κατὰ … φάγωσιν is tmesis for κατεσθίω 'eat up'. δασσάμενοι is the aorist participle of δατέομαι 'divide', with epic σσ. τηϋσίην means 'vain, fruitless'; its derivation is not agreed. Menelaus, whose late homecoming Nestor has just told, is the example behind the warning.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἐς μὲν Μενέλαον ἐγὼ κέλομαι καὶ ἄνωγα
ἐλθεῖν·
sentences.tr:
all’ es men Menelaon egō kelomai kai anōga
elthein·
sentences.l:
But to Menelaus I bid and urge you
to go;
sentences.i: But I bid you, and I urge you, to go to Menelaus;
sentences.n: κέλομαι is an epic verb, 'bid, order'. ἄνωγα is a perfect with present sense, 'command'; the two verbs together give the advice its weight. ἐς Μενέλαον is 'to Menelaus', with ἐς of motion towards a person. μέν has no answering δέ; after ἀλλά it marks this as the one thing Telemachus should do. The infinitive ἐλθεῖν is held over to the head of line 318, and the raised point follows it at once.

sentences.t:
κεῖνος γὰρ νέον ἄλλοθεν εἰλήλουθεν,
ἐκ τῶν ἀνθρώπων, ὅθεν οὐκ ἔλποιτό γε θυμῷ
ἐλθέμεν, ὅν τινα πρῶτον ἀποσφήλωσιν ἄελλαι
ἐς πέλαγος μέγα τοῖον,
sentences.tr:
keinos gar neon allothen eilēlouthen,
ek tōn anthrōpōn, hothen ouk elpoito ge thymōi
elthemen, hon tina prōton aposphēlōsin aellai
es pelagos mega toion,
sentences.l:
for that man lately from elsewhere has come,
from those people, from whom one would not hope in his heart
to come home, whom once the storms have driven astray
into a sea so great,
sentences.i: for he has lately come home from abroad, from people from whose land no man would hope in his heart to return, once the storms had driven him off course into so great a sea,
sentences.n: The sentence runs from 318 to 322 without a stop, and is cut at the comma after τοῖον, where the statement about Menelaus is complete and a clause about the sea begins. κεῖνος is ἐκεῖνος. εἰλήλουθεν is the epic perfect of ἔρχομαι (Attic ἐλήλυθε). νέον 'lately' and ἄλλοθεν 'from elsewhere' are adverbs. ἔλποιτο is a potential optative without κε, which Homer allows. Its subject is the indefinite antecedent of ὅν τινα, 'whoever'. ἐλθέμεν is an infinitive in -έμεν. ἀποσφήλωσιν, aorist subjunctive of ἀποσφάλλω 'drive off course', stands without κε in a general relative clause. πρῶτον is 'once, as soon as'.

sentences.t:
ὅθεν τέ περ οὐδ’ οἰωνοὶ
αὐτόετες οἰχνεῦσιν, ἐπεὶ μέγα τε δεινόν τε.
sentences.tr:
hothen te per oud’ oiōnoi
autoetes oichneusin, epei mega te deinon te.
sentences.l:
from where not even birds
within the same year make their way, since it is vast and terrible.
sentences.i: a sea from which not even birds make their way within the year, so vast and terrible it is.
sentences.n: ὅθεν τέ περ has the epic τε of a standing fact, with περ 'even'. οἰωνοί are birds, properly large birds of prey and omen. αὐτόετες is an adverb from αὐτός and ἔτος, 'in the same year, within the year'. οἰχνεῦσιν is from οἰχνέω 'go, travel', with Ionic -εῦσι contracted from -έουσι. μέγα τε δεινόν τε, 'both vast and terrible', is neuter, agreeing with πέλαγος, and the verb 'is' is left out. The birds are Nestor's measure: even they cannot cross this sea within a year.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἴθι νῦν σὺν νηί τε σῇ καὶ σοῖς ἑτάροισιν·
sentences.tr: all’ ithi nyn syn nēi te sēi kai sois hetaroisin·
sentences.l: But go now, with both your ship and your companions;
sentences.i: So go now, with your ship and your companions;
sentences.n: ἴθι is the imperative of εἶμι 'go'. νηί is the dative singular of the epic νηῦς (Attic ναῦς). σῇ and σοῖς are forms of the possessive σός 'your'. ἑτάροισιν is a dative plural in -οισι(ν), from ἕταρος, the by-form of ἑταῖρος. τε … καί is 'both … and'. This is the sea route, with the ship and crew he came in; the land route is offered in the next lines.

sentences.t:
εἰ δ’ ἐθέλεις πεζός, πάρα τοι δίφρος τε καὶ ἵπποι,
πὰρ δέ τοι υἷες ἐμοί, οἵ τοι πομπῆες ἔσονται
ἐς Λακεδαίμονα δῖαν, ὅθι ξανθὸς Μενέλαος.
sentences.tr:
ei d’ etheleis pezos, para toi diphros te kai hippoi,
par de toi huies emoi, hoi toi pompēes esontai
es Lakedaimona dian, hothi xanthos Menelaos.
sentences.l:
And if you wish to go on foot, at hand for you are a chariot and horses,
and at hand for you are my sons, who will be your escorts
to heavenly Lacedaemon, where fair-haired Menelaus is.
sentences.i: Or if you would rather go by land, a chariot and horses are ready for you, and my sons are ready too, to be your escorts to heavenly Lacedaemon, where fair-haired Menelaus is.
sentences.n: πεζός is literally 'on foot', and so 'by land'. The English supplies the verb 'to go'. πάρα, accented on the first syllable, stands for πάρεστι or πάρεισι 'is, are at hand'. πὰρ in the next line is the same word shortened, and τοι 'for you' is repeated three times. δίφρος is properly the platform of a chariot, and so the chariot. Λακεδαίμων is the land in which Sparta lies. δῖος 'heavenly' is given to places as well as to persons; of the sea at 3.153 it was 'heavenly' in the line-for-line English but 'bright' in the reading English. ὅθι is 'where', and 'is' is left out.

sentences.t: λίσσεσθαι δέ μιν αὐτός, ἵνα νημερτὲς ἐνίσπῃ·
sentences.tr: lissesthai de min autos, hina nēmertes enispēi·
sentences.l: And beseech him yourself, so that he may tell you the unerring truth;
sentences.i: And entreat him yourself to tell you the unerring truth;
sentences.n: λίσσεσθαι is an infinitive used as an imperative, and αὐτός 'you yourself' agrees with its unexpressed subject. ἵνα with the subjunctive gives the purpose. νημερτές is the neuter of νημερτής 'unerring', used as the object, and ἐνίσπῃ is the aorist subjunctive of ἐνέπω 'tell', the verb of ἔννεπε in 1.1. At 3.19 Athena gave Telemachus the same advice about Nestor, with ὅπως νημερτέα εἴπῃ. Nestor now passes him on with it, and the English keeps 'beseech him yourself'. The words νημερτὲς ἐνίσπες closed Telemachus' plea at 3.98, and 'the unerring truth' is taken from there.

sentences.t: ψεῦδος δ’ οὐκ ἐρέει·
sentences.tr: pseudos d’ ouk ereei·
sentences.l: and a falsehood he will not speak;
sentences.i: he will not tell a falsehood;
sentences.n: These words are the same as at 3.20, where Athena said them of Nestor, and they take the same English. ἐρέει is the uncontracted future of the stem ἐρ- 'say' (Attic ἐρεῖ). ψεῦδος 'a falsehood' stands first for emphasis. The raised point separates the assurance from its reason.

sentences.t: μάλα γὰρ πεπνυμένος ἐστίν.
sentences.tr: mala gar pepnymenos estin.
sentences.l: for he is very prudent.”
sentences.i: for he is very prudent.”
sentences.n: At 3.20 this clause closed Athena's speech with ἐστί. Here the line ends ἐστίν, with the movable ν, and it closes Nestor's long reply, which began at 3.254. πεπνυμένος is a perfect participle belonging to πνέω, 'having breath, having wits', and so 'prudent'. It is the standing epithet of Telemachus, and at 3.20 it was said of Nestor. Here it is said of Menelaus as a plain predicate. The English keeps 'prudent' so that the echo can be heard.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’, ἠέλιος δ’ ἄρ’ ἔδυ καὶ ἐπὶ κνέφας ἦλθε.
sentences.tr: hōs ephat’, ēelios d’ ar’ edy kai epi knephas ēlthe.
sentences.l: So he spoke, and the sun then set, and darkness came on.
sentences.i: So he spoke; and the sun set, and darkness came on.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ is ὣς ἔφατο, 'so he spoke', the narrator's formula that closes a speech. ἠέλιος is the epic form of ἥλιος. ἔδυ is the root aorist of δύω 'sink', used of the sun setting. In ἐπὶ … ἦλθε the preverb stands apart from the verb, which is ἐπέρχομαι 'come on'; ἐπί may also be read as an adverb, 'on, upon them'. κνέφας is 'dusk, darkness'. The nightfall is the reason Athena gives for ending the feast.

sentences.t: τοῖσι δὲ καὶ μετέειπε θεά, γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη·
sentences.tr: toisi de kai meteeipe thea, glaukōpis Athēnē·
sentences.l: And among them spoke also the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena:
sentences.i: And among them the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena, spoke up as well:
sentences.n: The words τοῖσι δὲ καὶ μετέειπε introduced Halitherses at 2.157 and keep their English. τοῖσι is the pronoun, 'among them'. μετέειπε is the aorist of μετεῖπον 'speak among', with the epic ἔειπε (Attic εἶπε) inside the compound. καί is 'also', after Nestor. θεά, γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη fills the end of the line as in the reply formulas. The narrator names the goddess, though the company sees her in the shape of Mentor. The raised point leads into her speech.

sentences.t: ὦ γέρον, ἦ τοι ταῦτα κατὰ μοῖραν κατέλεξας·
sentences.tr: ō geron, ē toi tauta kata moiran katelexas·
sentences.l: “Old man, truly these things according to what is fitting you have recounted;
sentences.i: “Old man, you have indeed told all this as is fitting;
sentences.n: ὦ γέρον 'old man' is a respectful address to an elder, and she speaks as Mentor. ἦ τοι is 'truly, surely'. κατὰ μοῖραν is 'according to what is fitting'. μοῖρα is a share, so the phrase means 'in due measure, rightly'. κατέλεξας is the aorist of καταλέγω 'recount', the verb of the fixed κατάλεξον. It must be kept apart from καταλέξεται at 353, which comes from a different verb meaning 'lie down'.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε τάμνετε μὲν γλώσσας, κεράασθε δὲ οἶνον,
ὄφρα Ποσειδάωνι καὶ ἄλλοις ἀθανάτοισιν
σπείσαντες κοίτοιο μεδώμεθα·
sentences.tr:
all’ age tamnete men glōssas, keraasthe de oinon,
ophra Poseidaōni kai allois athanatoisin
speisantes koitoio medōmetha·
sentences.i: But come, cut out the tongues and mix the wine, so that when we have poured libations to Poseidon and the other immortals we may think of our beds;
sentences.n: ἄγε 'come' is an imperative used as an interjection. τάμνετε is the epic form of τέμνετε 'cut'. The γλῶσσαι are the tongues of the sacrificed bulls, which are burnt at 341. κεράασθε is a present imperative middle of the verb 'mix', with the vowel stretched out (= κερᾶσθε). Wine was mixed with water in a mixing-bowl. ὄφρα 'so that' takes the subjunctive μεδώμεθα, from μέδομαι 'think of', which governs the genitive κοίτοιο 'bed, rest'. σπείσαντες is the aorist participle of σπένδω 'pour a libation'. Poseidon comes first because the day's feast was his sacrifice, which Telemachus found on the shore at 3.5.

sentences.t: τοῖο γὰρ ὥρη.
sentences.tr: toio gar hōrē.
sentences.l: for it is the hour for it.
sentences.i: for it is time for that.
sentences.n: τοῖο is the pronoun in a genitive in -οιο (Attic τοῦ), 'of it', meaning rest. ὥρη has Ionic η for Attic ὥρα 'season, the right time', and with a genitive it means 'the time for'. The verb 'is' is left out. The half-line ends at a raised point, and the reason for her advice follows.

sentences.t: ἤδη γὰρ φάος οἴχεθ’ ὑπὸ ζόφον, οὐδὲ ἔοικεν·
sentences.tr: ēdē gar phaos oicheth’ hypo zophon, oude eoiken·
sentences.l: For already the light has gone off beneath the gloom, and it is not fitting;
sentences.i: The light has already gone down into the gloom, and it is not fitting:
sentences.n: φάος is the uncontracted form of Attic φῶς 'light'. οἴχεθ’ is οἴχεται, 'is gone', a present with perfect sense, elided and aspirated before ὑπό. ζόφος is 'gloom, darkness', especially the dark of the west where the sun goes down. οὐδὲ ἔοικεν, 'nor is it fitting', is impersonal. The edition prints a raised point after it, which cuts the verb off from the infinitives in the next line that depend on it. The unit follows the edition's punctuation, and the English carries the sense across.

sentences.t: δηθὰ θεῶν ἐν δαιτὶ θαασσέμεν, ἀλλὰ νέεσθαι.
sentences.tr: dētha theōn en daiti thaassemen, alla neesthai.
sentences.l: long at the feast of the gods to sit, but to go home.”
sentences.i: we should not sit on long at the feast of the gods, but go home.”
sentences.n: These infinitives complete οὐδὲ ἔοικεν in the line before. δηθά is 'for long'. θαασσέμεν is an infinitive in -έμεν from θαάσσω, an epic form of θάσσω 'sit'. θεῶν ἐν δαιτί is 'at the gods' feast': the meal was a sacrifice, and the gods had their share of it. After ἀλλά the positive 'it is fitting' has to be understood from οὐδὲ ἔοικεν: it is right 'to go home'. νέεσθαι is uncontracted (Attic νεῖσθαι). Athena's speech ends here.

sentences.t: ἦ ῥα Διὸς θυγάτηρ, οἱ δ’ ἔκλυον αὐδησάσης.
sentences.tr: ē rha Dios thygatēr, hoi d’ eklyon audēsasēs.
sentences.l: She spoke, the daughter of Zeus, and they heard her speaking.
sentences.i: So said the daughter of Zeus, and they listened to her words.
sentences.n: ἦ is from the old verb ἠμί 'say', found almost only in this form, and like ὣς φάτο it closes a speech. ῥα is a worn-down ἄρα. Διὸς θυγάτηρ is the narrator's name for Athena, and the company still sees Mentor. οἱ δέ is the pronoun, 'and they'. ἔκλυον, from κλύω 'hear', takes the genitive of the person heard, with the aorist participle αὐδησάσης, from αὐδάω 'speak': 'heard her as she spoke'. κλύω often implies heeding, and they at once do what she proposed.

sentences.t:
τοῖσι δὲ κήρυκες μὲν ὕδωρ ἐπὶ χεῖρας ἔχευαν,
κοῦροι δὲ κρητῆρας ἐπεστέψαντο ποτοῖο,
νώμησαν δ’ ἄρα πᾶσιν ἐπαρξάμενοι δεπάεσσι·
sentences.tr:
toisi de kērykes men hydōr epi cheiras echeuan,
kouroi de krētēras epestepsanto potoio,
nōmēsan d’ ara pasin eparxamenoi depaessi·
sentences.i: And the heralds poured water over their hands, and young men filled the mixing-bowls to the brim with drink and served it out to all, first pouring a few drops into each cup;
sentences.n: Lines 338 and 339 repeat 1.146 and 1.148 word for word and keep the same English. The line about bread at 1.147 has no place here, since the company has already eaten and is now making ready the libations. The heralds serve at the feast. ἐπεστέψαντο is the aorist middle of ἐπιστέφω 'fill to the brim', with the genitive ποτοῖο 'with drink'. νώμησαν is the unaugmented aorist of νωμάω 'deal out'. ἐπαρξάμενοι δεπάεσσι is from ἐπάρχομαι 'make a beginning': a little wine was first poured into each cup for the libation. δεπάεσσι is a dative plural in -εσσι of δέπας 'cup'.

sentences.t: γλώσσας δ’ ἐν πυρὶ βάλλον, ἀνιστάμενοι δ’ ἐπέλειβον.
sentences.tr: glōssas d’ en pyri ballon, anistamenoi d’ epeleibon.
sentences.l: and the tongues into the fire they threw, and standing up they poured libations over them.
sentences.i: They threw the tongues into the fire, and standing up they poured libations over them.
sentences.n: These are the tongues that Athena told them to cut at 332. βάλλον is an unaugmented imperfect. ἐν πυρί, with ἐν and the dative after a verb of motion, is 'into the fire'; Homer often uses ἐν so. ἀνιστάμενοι is 'rising up' from their seats for the libation. ἐπέλειβον is the imperfect of ἐπιλείβω 'pour over', and the object is the wine, poured onto the tongues in the fire.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ σπεῖσάν τ’ ἔπιον θ’, ὅσον ἤθελε θυμός,
δὴ τότ’ Ἀθηναίη καὶ Τηλέμαχος θεοειδὴς
ἄμφω ἱέσθην κοίλην ἐπὶ νῆα νέεσθαι.
sentences.tr:
autar epei speisan t’ epion th’, hoson ēthele thymos,
dē tot’ Athēnaiē kai Tēlemachos theoeidēs
amphō hiesthēn koilēn epi nēa neesthai.
sentences.l:
But when they had poured libations and drunk, as much as their heart wished,
then indeed Athena and Telemachus godlike-in-form
both were eager to go back to the hollow ship.
sentences.i: But when they had poured libations and drunk as much as their hearts wished, then Athena and Telemachus, godlike in form, were both eager to go back to the hollow ship.
sentences.n: Line 342 comes again at 395 and takes the same English there. σπεῖσαν is an unaugmented aorist (Attic ἔσπεισαν), and ἔπιον is the aorist of πίνω. τ’ … θ’ are τε … τε, the second aspirated before ὅσον. ὅσον ἤθελε θυμός is 'as much as the heart wished'. δὴ τότ’ is 'just then'. Ἀθηναίη is a longer form of Ἀθήνη. The narrator names her, though she still looks like Mentor. ἱέσθην is a dual imperfect middle of ἵημι, 'were eager', with ἄμφω 'both' and the infinitive νέεσθαι.

sentences.t: Νέστωρ δ’ αὖ κατέρυκε καθαπτόμενος ἐπέεσσιν·
sentences.tr: Nestōr d’ au kateryke kathaptomenos epeessin·
sentences.l: But Nestor in turn held them back, accosting them with words:
sentences.i: But Nestor held them back, addressing them directly with these words:
sentences.n: αὖ is 'in turn'. κατέρυκε is the unaugmented imperfect of κατερύκω 'hold back', the verb used at 1.55 of Calypso detaining Odysseus. The imperfect suggests an attempt: he tried to keep them. καθαπτόμενος is 'accosting'. καθάπτομαι is 'lay hold of', and so 'address pointedly', and need not carry reproach. Here the pressure is a host's. ἐπέεσσιν is a dative plural in -εσσι of ἔπος 'word'. The raised point introduces the speech.

sentences.t:
Ζεὺς τό γ’ ἀλεξήσειε καὶ ἀθάνατοι θεοὶ ἄλλοι,
ὡς ὑμεῖς παρ’ ἐμεῖο θοὴν ἐπὶ νῆα κίοιτε
ὥς τέ τευ ἦ παρὰ πάμπαν ἀνείμονος ἠδὲ πενιχροῦ,
sentences.tr:
Zeus to g’ alexēseie kai athanatoi theoi alloi,
hōs hymeis par’ emeio thoēn epi nēa kioite
hōs te teu ē para pampan aneimonos ēde penichrou,
sentences.l:
“May Zeus ward this off, and the other immortal gods,
that you from me to the swift ship should go
as though from someone truly utterly without clothing and poor,
sentences.i: “May Zeus and the other immortal gods keep this from happening, that you should leave me for the swift ship as if you were leaving someone utterly without clothing and poor,
sentences.n: ἀλεξήσειε is the aorist optative of ἀλέξω 'ward off', in a wish. τό γε points forward to the ὡς-clause, 'this, namely that …', and κίοιτε, the optative of κίω 'go', takes the mood of the wish. ἐμεῖο is the epic genitive of ἐγώ (Attic ἐμοῦ). τευ is τινος, and παρά 'from (the house of)' governs τευ … ἀνείμονος. ἦ, accented so in the edition, is the affirming particle 'truly', giving weight to the whole description that follows rather than to πάμπαν alone. ἀνείμων is 'without clothing' (εἷμα), and πενιχρός 'poor'. The sentence runs to 350; the cut falls where the relative clause about the poor man begins.

sentences.t:
ᾧ οὔ τι χλαῖναι καὶ ῥήγεα πόλλ’ ἐνὶ οἴκῳ,
οὔτ’ αὐτῷ μαλακῶς οὔτε ξείνοισιν ἐνεύδειν.
sentences.tr:
hōi ou ti chlainai kai rhēgea poll’ eni oikōi,
out’ autōi malakōs oute xeinoisin eneudein.
sentences.l:
who has not any cloaks and rugs, many, in his house,
for either himself softly or his guests to sleep in.
sentences.i: a man who has no store of cloaks and rugs in his house for himself or his guests to sleep in softly.
sentences.n: ᾧ is a dative of the possessor, 'to whom there are', meaning 'who has'. οὔ τι is 'not any'. χλαῖναι are thick woollen cloaks, which also served as blankets. ῥήγεα, from ῥῆγος, are rugs or coverlets laid on a bed. πόλλ’ is πολλά, and ἐνί is ἐν. ἐνεύδειν 'sleep in them' is an infinitive of purpose, and μαλακῶς 'softly' goes with it. ξείνοισιν is 'guests'. Bedding for a guest was part of what a host owed.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ἐμοὶ πάρα μὲν χλαῖναι καὶ ῥήγεα καλά.
sentences.tr: autar emoi para men chlainai kai rhēgea kala.
sentences.l: But for me there are at hand cloaks and rugs, fine ones.
sentences.i: But I have cloaks and fine rugs at hand.
sentences.n: πάρα, accented on its first syllable, stands for πάρεισι 'are at hand', as at 324. ἐμοί is a dative of the possessor, and the English turns it into 'I have'. μέν stands alone, stressing 'I at any rate', against the poor man of the lines before. ῥήγεα καλά repeats the words of 349 with a new adjective: the rugs are not only there but fine.

sentences.t:
οὔ θην δὴ τοῦδ’ ἀνδρὸς Ὀδυσσῆος φίλος υἱὸς
νηὸς ἐπ’ ἰκριόφιν καταλέξεται, ὄφρ’ ἂν ἐγώ γε
ζώω, ἔπειτα δὲ παῖδες ἐνὶ μεγάροισι λίπωνται,
ξείνους ξεινίζειν, ὅς τίς κ’ ἐμὰ δώμαθ’ ἵκηται.
sentences.tr:
ou thēn dē toud’ andros Odyssēos philos huios
nēos ep’ ikriophin katalexetai, ophr’ an egō ge
zōō, epeita de paides eni megaroisi lipōntai,
xeinous xeinizein, hos tis k’ ema dōmath’ hikētai.
sentences.l:
Surely not, I warrant, will this man Odysseus' dear son
on a ship's deck lie down, so long as I at least
live, and after that children are left in my halls
to entertain strangers, whoever comes to my house.”
sentences.i: Surely the dear son of such a man as Odysseus will not lie down on a ship's deck, so long as I live and, after me, my sons are left in the halls to entertain strangers, whoever comes to my house.”
sentences.n: θην is an emphatic particle, 'surely, I warrant'. τοῦδ’ ἀνδρός, 'of this man', points to Odysseus as one much in mind. ἰκριόφιν adds -φι(ν) to ἴκρια 'deck', the half-decks at bow and stern. καταλέξεται is from καταλέγομαι 'lie down', of the root of λέχος 'bed'. ὄφρ’ ἄν takes the subjunctives ζώω (= ζῶ) and λίπωνται, 'as long as'. ξείνους ξεινίζειν is an infinitive of purpose, 'to entertain guests'. ὅς τίς κ’ with the subjunctive is 'whoever'. δώμαθ’ is δώματα, with θ before the rough breathing of ἵκηται.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε θεά, γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aute proseeipe thea, glaukōpis Athēnē·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena:
sentences.i: Then the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena, spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: The whole line is the reply formula already met at 1.178, and it takes the same English. τόν is the pronoun 'him', here Nestor. αὖτε is 'in turn'. προσέειπε is the aorist of προσεῖπον 'address', with the epic ἔειπε. The goddess answers in the shape of Mentor, and the narrator, as before, calls her by her own name.

sentences.t: εὖ δὴ ταῦτά γ’ ἔφησθα, γέρον φίλε·
sentences.tr: eu dē tauta g’ ephēstha, geron phile·
sentences.l: “Well indeed have you said this, dear old man;
sentences.i: “You have spoken well in this, dear old man;
sentences.n: ἔφησθα is the second person singular imperfect of φημί, with the old ending -σθα. δή strengthens εὖ, 'well indeed'. γε limits her agreement: 'this, at any rate', before she changes his plan for her own part. γέρον φίλε adds φίλε 'dear' to the fixed address 'old man' and makes it warmer. As Mentor, Athena speaks to Nestor as one old man to another.

sentences.t:
σοὶ δὲ ἔοικεν
Τηλέμαχον πείθεσθαι, ἐπεὶ πολὺ κάλλιον οὕτως.
sentences.tr:
soi de eoiken
Tēlemachon peithesthai, epei poly kallion houtōs.
sentences.l:
and it is fitting that to you
Telemachus should be obedient, since far better it is so.
sentences.i: and it is fitting that Telemachus should do as you say, for that is far the better way.
sentences.n: ἔοικεν is impersonal, 'it is fitting'. Τηλέμαχον is the accusative subject of the infinitive πείθεσθαι 'obey', and σοί, set first for emphasis, is the dative of the person obeyed. The line-for-line English keeps σοί first with 'to you … should be obedient'. κάλλιον is the comparative of καλός, 'finer, better', and πολύ is 'by far'. οὕτως 'so' stands beside οὕτω at 315; Homer uses both.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ οὗτος μὲν νῦν σοὶ ἅμ’ ἕψεται, ὄφρα κεν εὕδῃ
σοῖσιν ἐνὶ μεγάροισιν·
sentences.tr:
all’ houtos men nyn soi ham’ hepsetai, ophra ken heudēi
soisin eni megaroisin·
sentences.l:
But he now will go along with you, so that he may sleep
in your halls;
sentences.i: So he will go with you now, to sleep in your halls;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ is 'well then', turning from agreement to a plan. οὗτος is 'this man here', Telemachus. ἅμ’ is ἅμα 'together with', with the dative σοί. ἕψεται is the future of ἕπομαι 'follow, go along with'. ὄφρα κεν with the subjunctive εὕδῃ is 'so that he may sleep'. σοῖσιν ἐνὶ μεγάροισιν, 'in your halls', has the possessive σός, datives in -οισι(ν), and ἐνί for ἐν. The halls are plural for one house.

sentences.t:
ἐγὼ δ’ ἐπὶ νῆα μέλαιναν
εἶμ’, ἵνα θαρσύνω θ’ ἑτάρους εἴπω τε ἕκαστα.
sentences.tr:
egō d’ epi nēa melainan
eim’, hina tharsynō th’ hetarous eipō te hekasta.
sentences.l:
and I to the black ship
will go, so that I may cheer the companions and tell them each thing.
sentences.i: and I will go to the black ship, to cheer our companions and tell them everything.
sentences.n: εἶμ’ is εἶμι 'I shall go', a present with future sense, as in Attic. νῆα is the accusative of νηῦς (Attic ναῦν). Ships are 'black' from the pitch on their hulls. ἵνα takes two subjunctives, θαρσύνω 'encourage' and εἴπω 'tell'. θ’ … τε are τε … τε, the first elided and aspirated before ἑτάρους. ἕκαστα is 'each thing, everything'. The companions are the crew of Telemachus' ship, waiting on the shore.

sentences.t: οἶος γὰρ μετὰ τοῖσι γεραίτερος εὔχομαι εἶναι·
sentences.tr: oios gar meta toisi geraiteros euchomai einai·
sentences.l: For alone among them I claim to be the older;
sentences.i: For I claim to be the only older man among them;
sentences.n: οἶος, with smooth breathing, is 'alone'. μετὰ τοῖσι is 'among them', with the pronoun. γεραίτερος is the comparative of γεραιός 'old', the word used of Nestor at 373: 'older, an elder'. εὔχομαι here is 'declare, profess myself'. The same verb means 'pray' at 394, where Nestor prays to Athena, and Homer uses it in both ways. Athena is speaking as Mentor, the old companion of Odysseus.

sentences.t:
οἱ δ’ ἄλλοι φιλότητι νεώτεροι ἄνδρες ἕπονται,
πάντες ὁμηλικίη μεγαθύμου Τηλεμάχοιο.
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ alloi philotēti neōteroi andres hepontai,
pantes homēlikiē megathymou Tēlemachoio.
sentences.l:
and the others, younger men, follow out of friendship,
all of them the age-fellows of great-hearted Telemachus.
sentences.i: and the others, younger men, have come along out of friendship, all of them of an age with great-hearted Telemachus.
sentences.n: οἱ δ’ ἄλλοι, 'but the others', answers οἶος in the line before. φιλότητι is a dative of cause, 'out of friendship'. νεώτεροι is the comparative of νέος 'young'. ὁμηλικίη is a noun, 'those of the same age', with Ionic η, in apposition to πάντες: 'all of them the age-group of …'. μεγαθύμου Τηλεμάχοιο has a genitive in -οιο. μεγάθυμος is 'great-hearted', translated as it is wherever it occurs.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα κε λεξαίμην κοίλῃ παρὰ νηὶ μελαίνῃ
νῦν·
sentences.tr:
entha ke lexaimēn koilēi para nēi melainēi
nyn·
sentences.l:
There I would lie down, beside the hollow black ship,
now;
sentences.i: There I mean to lie down for tonight, beside the hollow black ship;
sentences.n: ἔνθα is 'there'. κε with the optative λεξαίμην is a potential, 'I would lie down', and in Homer it can state an intention politely. λεξαίμην is the aorist optative middle 'lie down', from the root of λέχος 'bed', like καταλέξεται at 353. κοίλῃ and μελαίνῃ, 'hollow' and 'black', are both standing epithets of ships, and νηί is the dative of νηῦς. νῦν stands alone at the head of line 366, 'for now', against ἠῶθεν 'at dawn' in the next clause.

sentences.t:
ἀτὰρ ἠῶθεν μετὰ Καύκωνας μεγαθύμους
εἶμ’ ἔνθα χρεῖός μοι ὀφέλλεται, οὔ τι νέον γε
οὐδ’ ὀλίγον.
sentences.tr:
atar ēōthen meta Kaukōnas megathymous
eim’ entha chreios moi ophelletai, ou ti neon ge
oud’ oligon.
sentences.l:
but at dawn to the great-hearted Caucones
I will go, where a debt is owed to me, not a new one at all
nor a small one.
sentences.i: but at dawn I will go to the great-hearted Caucones, where a debt is owed to me, and no new or small one either.
sentences.n: ἀτάρ is a by-form of αὐτάρ 'but'. ἠῶθεν is ἠώς 'dawn' with -θεν, 'from dawn, at dawn'. μετά with the accusative is 'to, among'. The Caucones are a people named here without further description. μεγαθύμους is 'great-hearted' again. χρεῖος is the epic form of χρέος 'debt', and ὀφέλλεται is an epic form of ὀφείλεται 'is owed'. οὔ τι νέον γε οὐδ’ ὀλίγον is litotes: an old debt and a large one. The errand gives Athena, in Mentor's person, a plain reason for leaving.

sentences.t:
σὺ δὲ τοῦτον, ἐπεὶ τεὸν ἵκετο δῶμα,
πέμψον σὺν δίφρῳ τε καὶ υἱέι·
sentences.tr:
sy de touton, epei teon hiketo dōma,
pempson syn diphrōi te kai huiei·
sentences.l:
But you, this man, since he has come to your house,
send on with a chariot and a son;
sentences.i: But since this man has come to your house, send him on his way with a chariot and one of your sons;
sentences.n: τοῦτον is 'this man', Telemachus, placed early as the object of πέμψον. τεόν is the epic form of σόν 'your'. ἵκετο is the aorist of ἱκνέομαι 'come'. The metre here needs a long ι, and that lengthening is the augment, which the spelling cannot show; the subjunctive ἵκηται at 355 has the short ι of the stem. πέμψον is the aorist imperative of πέμπω 'send on one's way, escort', the verb behind πομπῆες at 325. υἱέι is a dative singular of υἱός, from the stem υἱε-. The instruction takes up Nestor's own offer at 324–326 of a chariot and his sons.

sentences.t:
δὸς δέ οἱ ἵππους,
οἵ τοι ἐλαφρότατοι θείειν καὶ κάρτος ἄριστοι.
sentences.tr:
dos de hoi hippous,
hoi toi elaphrotatoi theiein kai kartos aristoi.
sentences.l:
and give him horses,
which of yours are lightest in running and best in strength.”
sentences.i: and give him horses, the lightest of foot you have and the best in strength.”
sentences.n: δός is the aorist imperative of δίδωμι, and οἱ is 'to him'. In the relative clause τοι is a dative of the possessor, 'your'. ἐλαφρότατοι is the superlative of ἐλαφρός 'light, nimble'. θείειν, the epic infinitive of θέω 'run' (Attic θεῖν), says in what respect they are lightest. κάρτος is κράτος with the letters transposed, an accusative of respect, 'best in strength'. Athena's speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα φωνήσασ’ ἀπέβη γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη
φήνῃ εἰδομένη·
sentences.tr:
hōs ara phōnēsas’ apebē glaukōpis Athēnē
phēnēi eidomenē·
sentences.l:
So then having spoken, gleaming-eyed Athena went away,
likened to a sea-eagle;
sentences.i: So she spoke, and gleaming-eyed Athena departed in the likeness of a sea-eagle;
sentences.n: In ὣς ἄρα φωνήσασ’, 'so then having spoken', φωνήσασ’ is the elided aorist participle of φωνέω. ἀπέβη is the aorist of ἀποβαίνω 'go away'. εἰδομένη with the dative is 'likened to', the participle used of her taking Mentor's shape. What bird φήνη was is not known. Sea-eagle, osprey and lammergeier have all been proposed, and 'sea-eagle' is used here only as a name. εἰδομένη was used of a real change of shape at 2.268, which favours taking her to become the bird, but the participle can also mean only 'resembling', and the words alone do not settle whether she becomes the bird or goes off like one.

sentences.t: θάμβος δ’ ἕλε πάντας ἰδόντας.
sentences.tr: thambos d’ hele pantas idontas.
sentences.l: and amazement took hold of all who saw.
sentences.i: Amazement seized all who saw it.
sentences.n: θάμβος is 'amazement', of the root of θαμβέω 'be astounded'. ἕλε is the unaugmented aorist of αἱρέω 'take, seize': the feeling is pictured as laying hold of the watchers. πάντας ἰδόντας, with the aorist participle of the stem ἰδ- 'see', is 'all who saw'. The departure shows everyone present that Mentor was a god in disguise.

sentences.t: θαύμαζεν δ’ ὁ γεραιός, ὅπως ἴδεν ὀφθαλμοῖσι·
sentences.tr: thaumazen d’ ho geraios, hopōs iden ophthalmoisi·
sentences.l: and the old man marvelled, when he saw it with his eyes;
sentences.i: and the old man marvelled when he saw it with his own eyes;
sentences.n: θαύμαζεν is an unaugmented imperfect. ὁ γεραιός is 'the old man'. Here ὁ comes close to the later article, but it still carries the sense 'he, the old one'. ὅπως is taken here as temporal, 'when'. It could also be read as 'at how he saw it'. ἴδεν is an unaugmented aorist. ὀφθαλμοῖσι is a dative plural in -οισι, 'with his eyes': Nestor has seen the goddess himself. The raised point leads into his reaction.

sentences.t: Τηλεμάχου δ’ ἕλε χεῖρα, ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζεν·
sentences.tr: Tēlemachou d’ hele cheira, epos t’ ephat’ ek t’ onomazen·
sentences.l: and of Telemachus he took the hand, and spoke a word, and called him by name:
sentences.i: and he took Telemachus by the hand, and spoke, calling him by name:
sentences.n: ἕλε χεῖρα with the genitive Τηλεμάχου is 'took Telemachus' hand'. The rest of the line is the closing half-line of the fixed two-line approach formula, used of Antinous at 2.302 and kept in the same English. ἔφατ’ is ἔφατο. ἔκ … ὀνόμαζεν is tmesis for ἐξονόμαζεν 'called by name', and here it ends in -εν, not -ε. Nestor's gesture is of a different kind from Antinous' at 2.302: it welcomes, and has no mockery in it.

sentences.t:
ὦ φίλος, οὔ σε ἔολπα κακὸν καὶ ἄναλκιν ἔσεσθαι,
εἰ δή τοι νέῳ ὧδε θεοὶ πομπῆες ἕπονται.
sentences.tr:
ō philos, ou se eolpa kakon kai analkin esesthai,
ei dē toi neōi hōde theoi pompēes hepontai.
sentences.l:
“O friend, I do not expect that you will be base and strengthless,
if indeed to you, so young, thus gods as escorts follow.
sentences.i: “Friend, I do not expect that you will turn out base or feeble, if the gods already attend you as escorts in this way, young as you are.
sentences.n: ὦ φίλος is a nominative used as a vocative. It is rendered as ὦ φίλ’ was at 3.103 and 3.211. ἔολπα is the perfect of ἔλπω with present sense, 'I expect'. κακόν is 'base, worthless', and in war 'cowardly'. ἄναλκιν is from ἄναλκις 'without ἀλκή', the strength to defend oneself. Of Aegisthus at 3.310 it was 'cowardly'; here the English keeps the literal sense. εἰ δή is 'if indeed', close to 'since'. νέῳ 'young' agrees with τοι. πομπῆες 'escorts' is the word Nestor used of his own sons at 325, and now it is the gods who escort Telemachus.

sentences.t:
οὐ μὲν γάρ τις ὅδ’ ἄλλος Ὀλύμπια δώματ’ ἐχόντων,
ἀλλὰ Διὸς θυγάτηρ, κυδίστη Τριτογένεια,
ἥ τοι καὶ πατέρ’ ἐσθλὸν ἐν Ἀργείοισιν ἐτίμα.
sentences.tr:
ou men gar tis hod’ allos Olympia dōmat’ echontōn,
alla Dios thygatēr, kydistē Tritogeneia,
hē toi kai pater’ esthlon en Argeioisin etima.
sentences.l:
For this was no other of those who hold the Olympian halls,
but the daughter of Zeus, most glorious Tritogeneia,
who also your noble father among the Argives used to honour.
sentences.i: For this was none other of those who hold the halls of Olympus but the daughter of Zeus, most glorious Tritogeneia, who also used to honour your noble father among the Argives.
sentences.n: οὐ … τις ἄλλος is 'no other'. ὅδ’ is 'this one', the figure who has just left. Ὀλύμπια δώματ’ ἐχόντων, 'of those who hold the Olympian halls', is a partitive genitive and stands for the gods. κυδίστη is a superlative from the root of κῦδος 'glory'. Τριτογένεια is a title of Athena whose meaning is not known. The ancients connected it with a lake or river Triton, with a word for 'head', or with 'third-born'. τοι is 'your'. ἐτίμα is a contracted imperfect, 'used to honour'. Ἀργεῖοι are the Greeks at Troy.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ ἄνασσ’ ἵληθι, δίδωθι δέ μοι κλέος ἐσθλόν,
αὐτῷ καὶ παίδεσσι καὶ αἰδοίῃ παρακοίτι·
sentences.tr:
alla anass’ hilēthi, didōthi de moi kleos esthlon,
autōi kai paidessi kai aidoiēi parakoiti·
sentences.l:
But, queen, be gracious, and give me good fame,
to myself and my children and my revered wife;
sentences.i: But, queen, be gracious, and grant a good name to me, to my children and to my revered wife;
sentences.n: Here Nestor turns from Telemachus to the goddess herself, and the speech becomes a prayer without any line from the narrator in between. ἄνασσ’ is the vocative of ἄνασσα 'queen, lady', the feminine of ἄναξ. ἵληθι is an epic imperative, 'be gracious'. δίδωθι is an epic imperative of δίδωμι (Attic δίδου). κλέος ἐσθλόν is 'good fame', as fixed. αὐτῷ 'myself' is in apposition to μοι. παίδεσσι is a dative plural in -εσσι. παράκοιτις 'wife' is literally 'she who lies beside', and αἰδοῖος is 'revered'.

sentences.t:
σοὶ δ’ αὖ ἐγὼ ῥέξω βοῦν ἦνιν εὐρυμέτωπον
ἀδμήτην, ἣν οὔ πω ὑπὸ ζυγὸν ἤγαγεν ἀνήρ·
sentences.tr:
soi d’ au egō rhexō boun ēnin eurymetōpon
admētēn, hēn ou pō hypo zygon ēgagen anēr·
sentences.l:
and to you in turn I will sacrifice a yearling heifer, broad-browed,
unbroken, which never yet under the yoke has a man led;
sentences.i: and in return I will sacrifice to you a yearling heifer, broad of brow and unbroken, one that no man has yet led under the yoke;
sentences.n: σοὶ δ’ αὖ, 'and to you in turn', offers the goddess a gift in exchange for the favour asked. ῥέξω is the future of ῥέζω 'do', which here means 'sacrifice'. βοῦν is feminine, 'a cow', and a young one, as the adjectives show. ἦνιν is usually explained as 'a year old', but the word is rare and its meaning is not certain. εὐρυμέτωπον is 'broad-browed', from εὐρύς and μέτωπον. ἀδμήτην is 'unbroken', from ἀ- and δάμνημι 'tame'. An animal never put to work was thought fit for a god.

sentences.t: τήν τοι ἐγὼ ῥέξω χρυσὸν κέρασιν περιχεύας.
sentences.tr: tēn toi egō rhexō chryson kerasin pericheuas.
sentences.l: Her I will sacrifice to you, gold around her horns having poured.”
sentences.i: I will sacrifice her to you, with gold poured around her horns.”
sentences.n: τήν 'her' is the pronoun, taking up the heifer. τοι is 'to you'. ῥέξω repeats the verb of 382 and the promise with it. περιχεύας is the aorist participle of περιχέω 'pour round', and its object is χρυσόν. κέρασιν is the dative plural of κέρας 'horn'. The horns of a victim were overlaid with gold before the sacrifice. Nestor's speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’ εὐχόμενος, τοῦ δ’ ἔκλυε Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη.
sentences.tr: hōs ephat’ euchomenos, tou d’ eklye Pallas Athēnē.
sentences.l: So he spoke, praying, and Pallas Athena heard him.
sentences.i: So he prayed, and Pallas Athena heard him.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ εὐχόμενος also closed Telemachus' prayer at 2.267 and takes the same English. τοῦ is the pronoun in the genitive with ἔκλυε 'heard': with κλύω the person heard is in the genitive. When a god 'hears' a prayer, the god attends to it with favour. The narrator states this outright, though he does not say what she grants. Παλλάς is a title of Athena. Its meaning is disputed: it has been linked with πάλλω 'brandish' and with πάλλαξ 'young girl'.

sentences.t:
τοῖσιν δ’ ἡγεμόνευε Γερήνιος ἱππότα Νέστωρ,
υἱάσι καὶ γαμβροῖσιν, ἑὰ πρὸς δώματα καλά.
sentences.tr:
toisin d’ hēgemoneue Gerēnios hippota Nestōr,
huiasi kai gambroisin, hea pros dōmata kala.
sentences.l:
And for them led the way the Gerenian horseman Nestor,
for his sons and sons-in-law, toward his own fine halls.
sentences.i: And the Gerenian horseman Nestor led the way for them, his sons and his sons-in-law, to his own fine halls.
sentences.n: τοῖσιν is the pronoun, 'for them', and υἱάσι καὶ γαμβροῖσιν in the next line says who they are. Telemachus goes with them. ἡγεμόνευε is the imperfect of ἡγεμονεύω 'lead the way', from ἡγεμών 'guide'. Γερήνιος ἱππότα Νέστωρ is Nestor's standing name-epithet, and the meaning of Γερήνιος is disputed. υἱάσι is an epic dative plural of υἱός. γαμβρός is 'son-in-law', and more loosely any kinsman by marriage. ἑά is the possessive ἑός 'his own', with δώματα plural for one house.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δώμαθ’ ἵκοντο ἀγακλυτὰ τοῖο ἄνακτος,
ἑξείης ἕζοντο κατὰ κλισμούς τε θρόνους τε·
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dōmath’ hikonto agaklyta toio anaktos,
hexeiēs hezonto kata klismous te thronous te·
sentences.l:
But when they reached the halls, the renowned ones, of that lord,
in order seated themselves along the seats and the chairs;
sentences.i: But when they came to the renowned halls of that lord, they took their places in order along the seats and the chairs;
sentences.n: Line 389 is the same as 1.145 and keeps its English. ὅτε is 'when'. δώμαθ’ is δώματα, with θ before the rough breathing of ἵκοντο. The metre gives ἵκοντο a short ι, so it is unaugmented here, unlike ἵκετο at 368. ἀγακλυτά is 'renowned', from the intensive ἀγα- and κλυτός 'famous'. τοῖο ἄνακτος, 'of that lord', has a genitive in -οιο. ἑξείης is 'in order, one after another'. κλισμοί and θρόνοι are two kinds of seat: the κλισμός has a back to lean on, and the θρόνος is a high chair.

sentences.t:
τοῖς δ’ ὁ γέρων ἐλθοῦσιν ἀνὰ κρητῆρα κέρασσεν
οἴνου ἡδυπότοιο, τὸν ἑνδεκάτῳ ἐνιαυτῷ
ὤιξεν ταμίη καὶ ἀπὸ κρήδεμνον ἔλυσε·
sentences.tr:
tois d’ ho gerōn elthousin ana krētēra kerassen
oinou hēdypotoio, ton hendekatōi eniautōi
ōixen tamiē kai apo krēdemnon elyse·
sentences.i: and for them, when they had come in, the old man mixed a bowl of wine sweet to drink, which the housekeeper opened in its eleventh year, loosing off its covering;
sentences.n: ἀνὰ … κέρασσεν is tmesis of ἀνακεράννυμι 'mix up'. κέρασσεν is an unaugmented aorist (Attic ἐκέρασε), with epic σσ, and κρητῆρα is the mixing-bowl. οἴνου is a partitive genitive, 'some of the wine'. ἡδυπότοιο is 'sweet to drink', from ἡδύς and the root of πίνω. ἑνδεκάτῳ ἐνιαυτῷ is a dative of time, 'in the eleventh year': the wine was opened when ten full years had passed since it was laid down. ὤιξεν is the aorist of οἴγνυμι 'open', with the augment turning οἰ- into ὠι-. κρήδεμνον is a woman's head-veil, and here the covering of the jar.

sentences.t:
τοῦ ὁ γέρων κρητῆρα κεράσσατο, πολλὰ δ’ Ἀθήνῃ
εὔχετ’ ἀποσπένδων, κούρῃ Διὸς αἰγιόχοιο.
sentences.tr:
tou ho gerōn krētēra kerassato, polla d’ Athēnēi
euchet’ apospendōn, kourēi Dios aigiochoio.
sentences.l:
Of it the old man mixed a bowl, and much to Athena
he prayed as he poured libation, to the daughter of aegis-bearing Zeus.
sentences.i: Of this wine the old man mixed a bowl, and as he poured the libation he prayed long to Athena, the daughter of aegis-bearing Zeus.
sentences.n: τοῦ, 'of it', is the wine just described. κεράσσατο is the unaugmented aorist middle and takes up the mixing of 390: the narrator returns to the bowl to lead into the libation. πολλά is adverbial, 'much, earnestly'. εὔχετ’ is εὔχετο, the imperfect, 'prayed'. It shows no augment (ηὐ- would), though Attic too often leaves εὐ- unchanged. ἀποσπένδων is 'pouring out a libation'. κούρῃ Διὸς αἰγιόχοιο is the fixed 'the daughter of aegis-bearing Zeus'. The meaning of αἰγίοχος is disputed; it is usually taken as 'holding the aegis', the goatskin shield of Zeus.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ σπεῖσάν τ’ ἔπιον θ’, ὅσον ἤθελε θυμός,
οἱ μὲν κακκείοντες ἔβαν οἶκόνδε ἕκαστος,
sentences.tr:
autar epei speisan t’ epion th’, hoson ēthele thymos,
hoi men kakkeiontes eban oikonde hekastos,
sentences.l:
But when they had poured libations and drunk, as much as their heart wished,
they, to lie down going, each one went to his own house,
sentences.i: But when they had poured libations and drunk as much as their hearts wished, the others each went off home to bed,
sentences.n: Line 395 is the same as 342 and keeps its English, and κακκείοντες ἔβαν οἶκόνδε ἕκαστος repeats 1.424 and keeps its English too. The sentence runs to 401 with only commas, and it is cut where the μέν-clause, about the guests who go home, gives way to the δέ-clause about Telemachus. κακκείοντες is κατακείοντες, with κατά shortened and assimilated. κείω is a future or desiderative form belonging to κεῖμαι: 'meaning to lie down, going to rest'. ἔβαν is the epic form of ἔβησαν. οἶκόνδε has -δε 'towards'. The singular ἕκαστος stands beside the plural verb.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ αὐτοῦ κοίμησε Γερήνιος ἱππότα Νέστωρ,
Τηλέμαχον, φίλον υἱὸν Ὀδυσσῆος θείοιο,
τρητοῖς ἐν λεχέεσσιν ὑπ’ αἰθούσῃ ἐριδούπῳ,
sentences.tr:
ton d’ autou koimēse Gerēnios hippota Nestōr,
Tēlemachon, philon huion Odyssēos theioio,
trētois en lecheessin hyp’ aithousēi eridoupōi,
sentences.l:
and him the Gerenian horseman Nestor put to bed there,
Telemachus, the dear son of divine Odysseus,
on a bored bedstead beneath the loud-echoing portico,
sentences.i: while the Gerenian horseman Nestor put Telemachus, the dear son of divine Odysseus, to bed there in the house, on a corded bedstead under the loud-echoing portico,
sentences.n: τὸν δ’ answers οἱ μέν: 'but him'. αὐτοῦ is an adverb, 'there, on the spot', in Nestor's own house. κοίμησε is the unaugmented aorist of κοιμάω 'put to bed'. λεχέεσσιν is a dative plural in -εσσι of λέχος 'bed', plural for one bed. τρητός is 'bored, pierced': the frame was bored with holes for the cords that carried the bedding. As at 1.440, the line-for-line English keeps 'bored' and the reading English says 'corded', naming what the holes were for. The αἴθουσα is the roofed portico of the house, and ἐρίδουπος is 'loud-echoing', from ἐρι- and δοῦπος 'thud'.

sentences.t:
πὰρ’ δ’ ἄρ’ ἐυμμελίην Πεισίστρατον, ὄρχαμον ἀνδρῶν,
ὅς οἱ ἔτ’ ἠίθεος παίδων ἦν ἐν μεγάροισιν·
sentences.tr:
par’ d’ ar’ eymmeliēn Peisistraton, orchamon andrōn,
hos hoi et’ ēitheos paidōn ēn en megaroisin·
sentences.l:
and beside him, then, Peisistratus of the good ash-spear, chief of men,
who of his sons was still unwed in his halls;
sentences.i: and beside him Peisistratus of the good ash-spear, chief of men, the one of his sons who was still unmarried and living in his halls;
sentences.n: πὰρ’ is παρά shortened, used as an adverb, 'beside him', and the edition prints it with an apostrophe. The accusatives still depend on κοίμησε. ἐυμμελίην is from ἐυμμελίης 'with a good ash-spear': μελίη is the ash tree, and so a spear of ash. Peisistratus, Nestor's son, has already welcomed the guests at 3.36. ὄρχαμος ἀνδρῶν, 'chief of men', is a title of rank. οἱ is 'his'. ἠίθεος is 'an unmarried young man', and παίδων is a partitive genitive, 'of his sons'.

sentences.t:
αὐτὸς δ’ αὖτε καθεῦδε μυχῷ δόμου ὑψηλοῖο,
τῷ δ’ ἄλοχος δέσποινα λέχος πόρσυνε καὶ εὐνήν.
sentences.tr:
autos d’ aute katheude mychōi domou hypsēloio,
tōi d’ alochos despoina lechos porsyne kai eunēn.
sentences.l:
And he himself in turn slept in the innermost part of the high house,
and for him his wife, the lady, made ready the bed and the bedding.
sentences.i: He himself slept in the innermost part of the high house, and his wife, the lady of the house, made ready the bed and the bedding for him.
sentences.n: αὐτός is Nestor himself, and αὖτε is 'in turn': the host goes to rest after his guest. καθεῦδε is an imperfect with no augment (Attic καθηῦδε or ἐκάθευδε). μυχῷ is a dative of place without a preposition, 'in the inmost part', and δόμου ὑψηλοῖο has a genitive in -οιο. τῷ is 'for him'. ἄλοχος is 'wife' and δέσποινα 'mistress of the house'; she is not named. πόρσυνε is an unaugmented past form of πορσύνω 'prepare'. Of a wife it has been taken to mean that she shares the bed too, but the words say only that she made it ready.
